title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: SOME ADJECTIVES DO NOT SHOW GENDER AT ALL. fortis is the shape for a man AND for a woman — fortis frāter and fortis soror — where L1's laetus had laetus and laeta. So an adjective's ending stops being a clue about who is being described: only the noun tells you, and this family is as common as the other.

This family has two shapes rather than three: fortis for a person of either gender, forte for a neuter thing. L1-M9 met trīstis once and said the family existed; here it is fortis, gravis and brevis, and the pattern is productive. A dictionary lists both shapes — fortis, forte — for exactly this reason.

gravis is 'heavy' and also 'serious', and of a person it means the second. English kept the word in 'grave' and 'gravity', which is a rare case of a cognate telling the truth — but it does NOT mean sad, which is L1-M9's trīstis.

Family words come in pairs and each pair is two separate words, not one word with two endings: frāter and soror, pater and māter. fīlius and fīlia are the exception — they ARE one word with two endings, like discipulus and discipula. Learn which is which, because it decides whether you can guess the other half.

-que joins the second of two things, and this module is where L1-M10's seam gets its textbook pair: pater māter-que, 'father and mother'. Printed Latin writes it solid — patermaterque is wrong but māterque is right — and this course keeps the hyphen so both halves stay visible. et does the same job in a separate word and is never wrong.

A fourth case appears, and only for relationships: fīlia magistrae est, 'she is the teacher's daughter'. The -ae is doing what English does with an apostrophe. Of a man it would be magistrī — which is also the word for 'teachers', so one spelling does two jobs and only the sentence tells you which.

quālis est asks 'what is he like?' and its answer is an adjective. It is itself one of this module's two-shape adjectives, which makes it a neat demonstration: quālis est magister? and quālis est magistra? are the same three words.

words.note: 'Brother'. Its pair is soror, 'sister' — a completely separate word, not frāter with a different ending, so knowing one does not give you the other.
'Brave, strong' — and the SAME shape for a man or a woman. Only forte, for a neuter thing, is different. English 'fortitude' and 'force' keep it.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: There is no 'my'. Latin leaves possession to the situation when it is obvious, exactly as it leaves out 'a' and 'the' — and a learner hunting for a word for 'my' is hunting for one this course has not taught.
sentences.sound: FRA-ter FOR-tis EST. The ā of frāter is long and stressed; fortis is two short syllables.

variations.changed: a woman, and the adjective does NOT change — which is the module's whole point
a different adjective of the same family
and a third, describing height rather than character

mistake.why: A feminine ending invented on laetus's model. fortis belongs to the family with no separate feminine — a woman is fortis, exactly as a man is — and forta is not a Latin word at all.

sentences.usage: Said about a member of your family.
sentences.mnemonic: fortis is the same for him and for her.

words.note: 'Sister', and its pair is frāter — two separate words. English 'sorority' keeps it, where 'fraternity' keeps the other.
'Serious' of a person and 'heavy' of a thing; gravēs of more than one. Same shape for a man or a woman; grave for a neuter thing. It does NOT mean sad — that is trīstis.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: gravis is not 'grave' in the English sense of grim. Of a person it is weighty, dignified, to be taken seriously — a compliment rather than a warning, which the cognate hides.
sentences.sound: SO-ror GRA-vis EST. Nothing long anywhere; the whole line is light and quick.

variations.changed: a man, and again the adjective does not move

mistake.why: An object ending on a word that is describing the subject. gravis follows soror, which is what the sentence is about, so it takes the subject shape — the object shape belongs in M3, where an adjective finally describes something being acted on.

sentences.mnemonic: gravis of a person is weighty; of a book it is heavy.

sentences.cue: My father and mother are here.

words.note: 'Father'. Its pair is māter — a separate word, like frāter and soror. English 'paternal' and 'patriot' keep it.
'And', and it behaves exactly as English does: between the two things, never joined on. The safe choice whenever you are unsure.
'Mother', with a long ā, and pater's pair. English 'maternal' and 'matrix' keep it. The next sentence joins it to pater with an enclitic instead of et.
'Here', with a LONG i. Its short twin hic means 'this' — one bar apart, and L1-M7 taught them together.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: Two people means sunt and not est. L1-M8 showed this with two books; here it is two people joined by et, and the verb answers to both of them together.
sentences.sound: PA-ter et MA-ter HEEK SUNT. The ā of māter is long and pater's a is not — one pair of words, one long vowel between them.

mistake.why: The verb left singular after two subjects. et joins them into a plural whatever their own shapes are, so sunt is the only possible verb — and this is the commonest agreement error in the module.

words.note: 'Father'. Its pair is māter — a separate word, like frāter and soror. English 'paternal' and 'patriot' keep it.
'And', hung on the SECOND of a pair — L1-M10's enclitic, and pater māter-que is its textbook use. Printed Latin joins it up: māterque.
'Here', with a LONG i. Its short twin hic means 'this' — one bar apart, and L1-M7 taught them together.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: This is S03 with one word fewer and the same meaning. -que and et are interchangeable here, and -que is what a Roman reaches for when the two things belong together — a pair of parents rather than two unrelated people.
sentences.sound: PA-ter MA-ter-que HEEK SUNT. The enclitic pulls the stress: māter alone is MA-ter, and with -que on it the beat moves to ma-TER-que.

mistake.why: The enclitic on the first of the pair. -que joins its host to what came BEFORE it, so on pater it has nothing to join — the sentence claims that the father is being added to something unmentioned.

sentences.usage: Said of two people who go together.

words.note: 'What is he like?' — itself a two-shape adjective, so quālis est magister? and quālis est magistra? are identical; quālēs for more than one. Its answer is an adjective.

'Teacher', carrying the teacher's gender: magister of a man, magistra of a woman, magistrī of more than one.

sentences.trap: No -ne and no helper. quālis already asks, so the question particle would be asking twice — the same rule ubi, quot and cūr each taught in L1.

mistake.why: The yes/no particle stacked on a question word. L1 said this three times about ubi, quot and cūr; quālis is the fourth, and the rule has not changed — -ne turns a statement into a question, and this is already one.

sentences.usage: Said when you want a description rather than a fact.
